item.title: Q1 — Dichotomous Key Branching & Taxonomic Resolution
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Taxonomic Keys & Identification

Dichotomous keys are essential tools in taxonomy. They consist of a series of statements, each highlighting a distinct morphological characteristic that may be true or false depending on the organism under observation. As the organism is compared with these statements, the key systematically directs the user through a decision tree, ultimately leading to a specific taxonomic classification.

Figure 1. Dichotomous tree model with three levels; T - true, F - false.

To determine the species of an unknown organism, referred to as X, you utilize a hypothetical dichotomous key with 10 levels, structurally similar to the one depicted in Figure 1. The final level of this tree provides a conclusive taxonomic identification, with no further branching points. The tree has a complete set of nodes without terminating branches before the final level.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Determining the species of an organism with more complex morphological structures than that of organism X using the provided key will take more than 9 steps.
B. The maximal number of species that could be identified with the key is 512.
C. An identification step at level 3 (counting from the top) has four times more possible final taxonomic outcomes than an identification step at level 5.
D. Consider three taxa A, B, and C. If A and B share a more recent common ancestor than A and C, then the paths along the dichotomous key leading to A and B will certainly diverge at an earlier step than the paths leading to A and C.

item.title: Q10 — Heterodimer Formation, Ligand Signaling, and Stem Cell Differentiation
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Cell Signaling & Communication Gene Regulation: Eukaryotic & Epigenetics

Proteins A and B form a heterodimer and only then do they induce stem cell differentiation. Protein A is regulated at the transcriptional level by transcription factor X, which is in turn regulated by the ligand L. On the other hand, protein B is regulated post-translationally through phosphorylation and dephosphorylation at serine-121 residue.

Figure 1. A Researchers isolated DNA-bound and unbound proteins (fractions) and analyzed the abundance of transcription factor X by Western Blot analysis but forgot to label the fractions. B Researchers studied how the deficiency of kinase and phosphatase affects the differentiation of cells by performing a Western Blot analysis. The higher the differentiation marker the higher the chance of differentiation. C The structures of phosphorylated serine and two other amino acids. Note that one amino acid can mimic phosphorylated serine.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. For quick cellular response, the regulation mechanism of protein B's activity is more energy-efficient than that of protein A's.
B. Ligand L reduces the affinity of transcription factor X to DNA.
C. Phosphorylation of protein B prevents the interaction of proteins A and B.
D. Mutating the serine-121 residue in protein B to aspartate likely causes the same effect on the formation of heterodimers as the activity of the kinase.

item.title: Q11 — Proteasome vs. Lysosome Degradation and Protein Half-Life
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Endomembrane System & Protein Trafficking

Proteasomes, cytoplasmic multiprotein complexes, and lysosomes are major proteolysis (protein degradation) sites in eukaryotic cells.

In Figure 1-a, researchers studied the abundance of proteins A, B, and C over time in cultured human cells using cycloheximide, an inhibitor of translation elongation in eukaryotic 80S ribosomes. Note that cycloheximide does not affect the abundance of protein A, whose half-life is shorter than that of protein B.

In Figure 1-b, they observed how MG132, a proteasome inhibitor, and chloroquine, a lysosome inhibitor, affect the abundance of proteins B and C over time under cycloheximide treatment.

Figure 1. 1-a Y: Protein abundance, X: Time (hours), I: Before adding cycloheximide, II: After adding cycloheximide, A: protein A, B: protein B, C: protein C. 1-b Y: Protein abundance, X: Time after adding cycloheximide (hours), B: protein B, C: protein C, N: control, M: MG132, Q: Chloroquine.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Cycloheximide treatment alone provides direct information on the rate of protein synthesis.
B. The half-life of protein B is shorter than the half-life of protein C.
C. Protein A is more likely to be mitochondrial than proteins B and C.
D. Protein B is more likely to be an extracellular protein than protein C.

item.title: Q12 — FRET-Based Protease Activity and Inhibitor Mechanism
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Biomolecular Analytical Techniques

Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) is a technique used to study the interaction between two chromophores, donor and acceptor. The donor (D) can be excited by light of a specific wavelength, raising the energy of an electron in the molecule. When far away from the acceptor (A), it will emit light via fluorescence. However, when it is within 10 nm of an acceptor molecule, it can “transfer” its energy to the acceptor, which then releases the absorbed energy as a different wavelength of light.

For an efficient FRET, the emission spectra of the donor must overlap with the excitation spectra of the acceptor. A table lists some chromophores’ excitation and emission spectra, including CFP and YFP. Researchers used FRET to find the optimal protease. Here, CFP and YFP fluorescent proteins are linked (CFP-YFP) with the protease-target peptide sequence. Researchers also observed the effect of two inhibitors on Protease P3 by using FRET. Note that one inhibitor is competitive, while the other is non-competitive.

Figure 1. A Scheme of regular fluorescence (1) and FRET (2). B Emission spectrum upon excitation of 5 samples. C Effect of two inhibitors on the activity of Protease P3 measured by FRET. Table 1. Excitation and emission spectra of some fluorophores.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. The probability of FRET decreases if the concentration of both donor and acceptor in the same solution is increased.
B. Using Brim43 as the acceptor, the most optimal donor is G8.
C. Protease P3 has the highest activity among tested proteases.
D. Z and Q are competitive and non-competitive inhibitors, respectively.

item.title: Q13 — Shelterin, the T-loop, and Chromosome Bridge Formation
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
DNA Repair & Recombination Cell Cycle, Mitosis & Meiosis

Telomeres are critical structures at the end of eukaryotic chromosomes, preventing the loss of genetic information during cellular divisions. Since telomeres resemble DNA breakpoints, they need to be protected from cellular DNA break repair mechanisms to prevent the ligation of the telomeric ends of different chromosomes. For that, a protein complex, shelterin, generates a structure shown in Figure 1B.

Figure 1. A, B Refer to the question text — the telomere’s single-stranded 3’ overhang (A) is tucked into a protective T-loop structure (B). C Microscopic images showing how factors X and Y affect the structure of chromosomes (one of the factors is a subunit of the shelterin complex). Telomeres are labeled with the green probe. D Microscopic images showing how unprotected telomeres result in chromosomal bridges during mitosis (white arrows point to the chromosome breakage, which starts at 6 min).

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. The structure shown in Figure 1B also protects telomeres from nucleases resolving meiotic recombination.
B. Factor Y is more likely to be involved in DNA break repair than factor X.
C. The bridged chromosome in Figure 1D has at least two centromeres.
D. The force generated by the kinetochore-associated microtubules physically breaks the bridged chromosome.

item.title: Q14 — Aral Sea Food-Chain Restoration and Salinity Tolerance
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Ecology

The Aral Sea, located in the southwest of Kazakhstan, was one of the largest salt lakes in the world before drying out. Today, the Aral Sea has two basins: Northern and Southern. Freshwater rivers: Syr Darya flows into the Northern basin and Amu Darya flows into the Southern basin. The water from Amu Darya is overused in agriculture, thus only a small part flows into the sea.

One way of restoring the biota of the Aral Sea is by introducing a food chain of new organisms into the sea. Note that species W and Z are native to the Aral Sea ecosystem, and also inhabit freshwater rivers flowing into the Aral Sea.

Figure 1. A The Aral Sea before and after. B Graph of changes in the salinity of both basins (mg/mL) and quantity metric of adult organisms (arbitrary units). A – salinity, W – species W, Z – species Z. The red arrow indicates the artificial introduction of a community of new species.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. A fish species introduced for biota restoration must feed on phytoplankton.
B. Species Z is more resistant to high salt concentrations than species W.
C. It's more likely that the return of species W happened earlier in the Northern Aral than in the Southern.
D. Among the artificially introduced animals, there were organisms that are prey for species Z but not predators of species Z.

item.title: Q15 — Lotka-Volterra Competition Lines and Coexistence Outcomes
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license

Ecology

The Lotka-Volterra model is used to predict the dynamics of competing populations. It is based on the following equations and is analyzed by constructing specific lines:

$$\frac{dN_1}{dt} = r_1 N_1 \left(\frac{K_1 - N_1 - \alpha N_2}{K_1}\right), \qquad \frac{dN_2}{dt} = r_2 N_2 \left(\frac{K_2 - N_2 - \beta N_1}{K_2}\right)$$

where K - carrying capacity, N - number of individuals, r - intrinsic rate of increase, α - competition coefficient of species 2 on species 1, β - competition coefficient of species 1 on species 2, and dN/dt = population growth rate.

The Lotka-Volterra line represents the number of individuals in a population at equilibrium (dN/dt = 0). For two species in competition, there are only 4 combinations of the location of these lines. Depending on the initial values of populations, the future changes in populations’ dynamics can be predicted.

Figure 1. A Lotka-Volterra lines. B Combinations of line locations and trends — arrows show the further direction of populations’ dynamics for particular initial values, indicated by blue dots.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. The y-intercept for line of species 1 is equal to K1/α.
B. This model takes into account the presence of intraspecific competition.
C. Suppose that there is a certain community of elks (K1 = 200, α = 1) and deer (K2 = 100, β = 2) competing with each other. If the current populations are 120 elks and 60 deer, the elks will eventually outcompete the deer.
D. In only 2 scenarios out of 4 described in Figure 1B both species can stably coexist.

item.title: Q16 — Niche Dimensions and Stipa capillata Drought Adaptation
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Ecology

The “hypothesis of intra-niche dimensions” states that stable coexistence in one ecological niche can be reached if the growth of one species is constricted by one limiting factor and the growth of a neighbour species by another. The balance of limiting factors creates trade-offs, allowing more than one species to occupy different “dimensions” within a niche; otherwise, a more adapted species will completely displace a less adapted one.

In the steppe conditions, Stipa capillata is more resistant to drought compared to other perennial grasses. However, since its root system is weak, it cannot spread vigorously in grasslands with good perennial turf.

Turf is a surface layer of soil, densely overgrown with short herbaceous plants very close to the ground.

Figure 1. Stipa capillata.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Based on the hypothesis, fast-growing plants usually overpopulate nutrient-poor soils.
B. Horses grazing in the meadows of Stipa grass can help increase the number of other plant species in the steppe.
C. Uncontrolled ploughing of steppe areas will lead to a decline in the biomass of Stipa grass relative to other perennial grasses.
D. During the drought season, the biomass of turf may decrease, particularly, owing to the reduced photosynthesis in turf.

item.title: Q17 — Incompatible Insect Technique and Wolbachia-Induced Cytoplasmic Incompatibility
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Ecology

The incompatible insect technique (IIT) controls harmful insects by inducing mating incompatibility with the use of Wolbachia bacteria. Wolbachia kills embryos only when an infected sperm fertilizes an uninfected egg, while other combinations show no developmental issues. Aedes albopictus is a mosquito species with males as active gamete dispersers. A study on IIT effectiveness began with collecting Wolbachia-free fertilized eggs from the wild. After being reared in the lab, newly hatched mosquitoes were irradiated to sterilize only females. All mosquitoes were then infected with Wolbachia and released into experimental sites, while control sites received wild-type mosquitoes. Hatched eggs were counted, with their spatial distribution shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1. Spatial distribution of hatched eggs. The red polygon marks the experimental site, and the blue polygon marks the control site. Yellow circles indicate the number of hatched eggs (larger circles denote more eggs).

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. The average lifespan of males of Aedes albopictus positively correlates with the effectiveness of IIT.
B. Reducing the initial irradiation dose can lead to resistance against the Wolbachia strain in successive mosquito generations.
C. When 50% of males and females are infected (1:1 sex ratio), 75% of matings produce no offspring due to cytoplasmic incompatibility.
D. Mosquito migration from control site to experimental site is the most likely explanation of the hatched eggs found in the experimental site.

item.title: Q18 — Ant Invasion, Visibility, and a Lion-Zebra-Buffalo Trophic Cascade
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Ecology

Symbiosis and trophic interactions are essential to maintain ecosystems. In this question, you will analyze the complex ecological relationship between whistling thorn trees, acacia ants (which receive nutrition and shelter from whistling thorn trees), megaherbivores (elephants), predators (lions), and their prey (zebras and buffalos) in an African savanna. You know that between 2000 and 2020, big-headed ants, an invasive ant species exterminating acacia ants, increased in number in the region.

Figure 1. A. Results showing how big-headed ant invasion affects visibility with (Y) or without (N) megaherbivores. The higher the number of whistling thorn trees, the lower the visibility. B. Results depicting how visibility affects zebra kill occurrence by lions. C. The proportion of prey (zebra or buffalo) killed by lions as a function of areal coverage of whistling thorn trees.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Based on the given data, the symbiosis between acacia ants and whistling-thorn trees is commensalism (only ants benefit from the interaction).
B. Zebras are more vulnerable to lion predation in big-headed ant-invaded areas.
C. Between 2000 and 2020, lions are expected to shift their prey from buffalos to zebras.
D. The study suggests that lions prefer ambushing zebras to chasing them for long distances.

item.title: Q19 — Heat-Balling Honeybee Defense Against Hornets
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Foraging & Anti-Predator Behavior

Honeybees like Apis cerana (Ac) and Apis mellifera (Am) defend against hornets (Vespa velutina, Vv) by forming a 44°C heat ball and stinging. The effects of heat (25°C or 44°C in thermostatic conditions) and stings from both species on hornet survival were studied. A mutant A. mellifera colony (Amdef) can generate heat but cannot sting and in all other aspects is similar to wild-type ones. Scientists also examined the body mass, venom mass, and stinger length of Ac, Am, and Vv. The figures below show data for wild-type bees.

Figure 1. A Graphs show the proportion of surviving hornets over time. p < 0.05 indicates statistical significance. B Body mass, venom mass, and stinger length for three species.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Venom mass is 2.6-2.8% of V. velutina's body mass.
B. Amdef bees can't kill any attacking V. velutina.
C. Amdef bees kill hornets as efficiently as the A. cerana species.
D. Over 3 hours at 44°C, the same number of A. cerana bees can kill more hornets than A. mellifera bees.

item.title: Q2 — Red Deer mtDNA Phylogeny & Bootstrap Support
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Molecular Systematics

There are many subspecies of Red Deer (Cervus elaphus) in Eurasia. The cytochrome b gene of mitochondrial DNA from 106 red deer samples, collected from different localities and representing different subspecies, was analyzed.

Figure 1. Red Deer in the National Park “Kölsay kölderi”.

Figure 2 shows part of the phylogenetic tree of Cervus samples based on the analysis of the mitochondrial DNA cytochrome b gene.

Figure 2. Phylogenetic tree of Red Deer. The numbers on each branch are called bootstrap values. They indicate how many times out of 100 iterations the same branch is observed when repeating the generation of a phylogenetic tree on a resampled set of data. (all the tips with numbers or letters indicate various groups of Cervus elaphus)

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. In 11 out of 100 bootstrap iterations Dama dama was not a sister group to Cervus spp.
B. Using the DNA of histone genes instead of mitochondrial DNA for construction of this phylogenetic tree would allow to better differentiate between deer subspecies.
C. Sample 163 is part of the most weakly supported branch in the tree.
D. A bootstrap value of 50 indicates the existence of only one alternative topology.

item.title: Q20 — Female Body Mass, Male Fighting, and Mating Outcomes in Crickets
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Mating Systems & Sexual Selection

Mating and male-to-male fighting in Gryllus bimaculatus are influenced by mating cost, sperm depletion, and female quality. Scientists studied the impact of female body mass on mating behavior and the effect of body mass differences in previous male-female encounters on male fighting outcomes. On average, females are heavier than males. Not all encounters led to successful copulation.

*Figure 1. A Female weight influence on mating outcome: copulated (1) and not copulated (2). B Body weight difference influence on male fighting outcomes: male winning (1) and male losing (2); median – solid line, boxes show 25% and 75% quartiles, p < 0.05. C Three hypothetical relationships between female fitness and the number of matings. Line 3 shows a system with an idealized relationship between female fitness and the number of matings. D G. bimaculatus.

On your answer sheet, indicate if the following statements are True (T) or False (F) based on the data provided.

A. The lighter the female, the more chances of being inseminated.
B. During male-to-male fights the heavier one on average wins more often.
C. Measurement of copulation duration is a good indicator of mating cost in terms of sperm depletion.
D. If we assume that female of species G. bimaculatus displays a type 1 fitness-mating relationship (Figure 1C), then smaller females will have lower fitness compared to large-sized ones.

item.title: Q21 — Cannibalism Probability and Injury Bias in Japanese Mitten Crabs
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license

Foraging & Anti-Predator Behavior

Japanese mitten crabs, Eriocheir japonica, can display cannibalistic behavior. The absence of other food resources can greatly facilitate cannibalism. As a result of this, some crabs might be injured or killed. Injury level is not limited to the number of lost extremities but also includes any other forms of it. Figure 1 (A,B) displays the probability of cannibalism versus Factor S:

$$\text{Factor } S = 1 - \frac{\text{prey size}}{\text{predator size}}$$

Figure 1-D shows hypothetical results.

*Figure 1. A,B Cannibalism among only male (graph A) and only female (graph B) crabs, n-number of crabs. C Y – mean (+SD) of Factor S among killed and injured groups, p<0.05. D Injured crabs’ occurrence frequencies.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Among male crabs, the cannibalism probability is 50% when predator to prey size ratio is about 1.75.
B. Females have a higher eagerness to cannibalism than males
C. In a cannibalistic environment, the occurrence of injured crabs will resemble the frequencies displayed in Figure 1D.
D. The difference in size affects whether the crab is killed or merely injured

item.title: Q22 — Genomic Imprinting at the IGF2-H19 Locus
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Extranuclear & Non-Mendelian Inheritance

Genomic imprinting is one mechanism by which sexes can encourage favourable traits in a fetus to maximize their own reproductive success. The most evident imprinting phenomenon occurs when the normal gene expression is disrupted.

Particularly, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) is characterized by fetal macrosomia (birth weight >90th percentile) and an increased risk of congenital tumors. Meanwhile, babies with Silver–Russell syndrome (SRS) are born small for their gestational age and later exhibit dwarfism.

Both cases can be associated with genetic defects in clusters of imprinted genes on chromosome 11. IGF2 is a pro-proliferative regulator of fetal growth. H19 knockout does not have pathological consequences. Another paternally imprinted gene (active on a maternal chromosome) is IGF2R; its protein binds IGF2 and targets it for lysosomal degradation.

Figure 1. Maternal and Paternal structures of the IGF2-H19 cluster. ICR - imprinting control region; En - Enhancer, Met - methylated, unMet - unmethylated.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. The figure implies that male infants are more often prone to cancers.
B. Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 11, both copies of the pair are inherited from a father, might lead to the symptoms of SRS.
C. Individuals with the maternal IGF2R loss of function will have the phenotype resembling that of the BWS patients.
D. The genome imprinting in monogamous species is expected to occur at lower rates than in polygamous species.

item.title: Q23 — ACE2/CTS1 Mutations and Multicellularity in Yeast
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Extensions of Mendelian Inheritance

Sometimes a formation of multicellular, organized structures can be observed in baker’s yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) in which newly divided yeast cells do not separate from the parent cell, illustrating a potential transition step from unicellular to multicellular organisms. The emergence of multicellular structures can be influenced by various factors, one of which is a mutation in the ACE2 gene, responsible for the transcriptional regulation of the protein-coding gene - CTS1. To investigate this, scientists crossed different yeast strains and sequenced ACE2 gene alleles.

Figure 1. A Wild type (G) and ACE2 mutant (H) yeast cells. The preparations were stained with dye for chitin. B Results of crosses between strains: blue - wild type, red - ACE2 mutants; R-multicellular, S-unicellular offspring. C Relative expression level of the CTS1 gene (black bar indicates the wild type, white and gray indicate two different strains with mutations in ACE2).

Figure 2. Ace2 gene region sequencing results; U - unknown.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. When subjected to identical incubation conditions, wild-type yeast cultures exhibit a faster settling rate compared to mutant yeast cultures.
B. The mutation in the yeast strain 8 causes a frameshift and is recessive.
C. The unknown sequencing sample in Figure 2 may be the offspring of a cross between strains 1 and 8.
D. The product of the CTS1 gene likely plays an important role in the final stages of cell division rather than in the initial stages.

item.title: Q24 — Robertsonian Translocation and Chromosome 14/21 Anomalies
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Chromosomal Variation: Number & Structure

Robertsonian translocation in human chromosomes occurs when recombination between two acrocentric chromosomes results in the fusion of two long arms and the loss of two short arms. Acrocentric chromosomes are characterized by centromeres positioned close to one end, resulting in notably short second arms. Obvious examples of such chromosomes in humans are chromosomes 14 and 21. Other acrocentric chromosomes have short arms of similar length and no banding pattern.

Table 1 shows information about anomalies associated with chromosomes 14 and 21, and Figure 1B displays the karyogram of one patient’s gamete.

Karyotype Phenotype
Trisomy 14 (2n + 1) Lethal
Trisomy 21 (2n + 1) Down syndrome
Monosomy 14 (2n - 1) Lethal
Monosomy 21 (2n - 1) Lethal
14-21 balanced translocation carrier (2n - 1) Normal

Table 1. Abnormalities of chromosomes 14 and 21.

Figure 1. A Robertsonian translocation mechanism. B Karyogram of a gamete.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. This type of translocation can also occur with chromosomes 1 and 2.
B. Not less than 50% of all possible embryos that can arise from the fusion of gametes from a father with Robertsonian translocation 14-21 and a healthy mother are lethal.
C. In order to determine the cause of the appearance of this karyogram in Figure 1B, it is necessary to carry out karyotyping of the patient's and his parents' somatic cells.
D. In total, 15 different types of Robertsonian translocations may occur in human cells.

item.title: Q25 — X-Linked Trait Allele Mixing and Pedigree Probability
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Sex Determination & Sex-Linked Inheritance Population Genetics & Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium

A unique phenotype associated with enhanced performance in labyrinth tasks has been identified in mice. The trait is X-linked.

Scientist A introduces 500 male and 500 female mice to an island. The initial allele frequencies in this population are p = 0.7 (dominant allele) and q = 0.3 (recessive allele). Subsequently, Scientist B brings another 500 male and 500 female mice which were drawn from a larger population with allele frequencies p=0.8, and q=0.2. Both the initial and final populations are assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. After several generations, the combined population on the island is 2,000 mice (Male/Female=1000/1000).

A female mouse was randomly picked up from Scientist A’s mice population before mixing and was crossed with Mouse 3 from the pedigree in Figure 1 (Cross Q).

Figure 1. Inheritance mode of “Performant” phenotype (black-colored). Mice have the same XX/XY system as humans.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

item.title: Q3 — BRCA1/53BP1 and DNA Double-Strand Break Repair Pathway Choice
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
DNA Repair & Recombination

DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) occur when both strands of the DNA molecule are broken, leading to cell death if not properly repaired. DSBs occur frequently and are primarily repaired through homologous recombination (HR) or non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ). As shown in Figure 1, the BRCA1 protein, when activated by DSBs, inhibits the 53BP1 protein, promoting the HR pathway. Alternatively, 53BP1 can be recruited to DSB sites, where it promotes the NHEJ pathway. Activation of either HR or NHEJ can be sufficient for cell survival. Figure 2 shows the level of BRCA1 protein and cell cycle profile of normal cells. 53BP1-deficient cells have similar BRCA1 protein and cell cycle profile as normal cells. 53BP1 protein level remains relatively same throughout the cell cycle in both normal and BRCA1-deficient cells. BRCA1 is required for the activation of the HR pathway regardless of the presence of 53BP1.

Figure 1. DSB repair pathways in normal cells. The red arrow indicates inhibition.

Figure 2. Normal cells were sampled over 20 hours and BRCA1 protein concentration relative to the maximum and the proportions of cells in various stages of cell cycle are analyzed. Y1 = BRCA1 protein (%). Y2 = % of Cells. X = Hours.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. The DSB repair pathway choice correlates with cell cycle status.
B. BRCA1-deficient cancer cells exhibit an increased reliance on the NHEJ pathway for DNA repair.
C. In normal cells, the HR pathway is more active in the G1 phase compared to the G2 phase.
D. Inhibitors of the transition from the G1 to the S phase will be more detrimental to 53BP1-deficient cells compared to BRCA1-deficient cells.

item.title: Q4 — Calcium Channel Signaling in Pancreatic Beta Cells
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Cell Signaling & Communication

A scientist in a lab is investigating two types of calcium channels in pancreatic beta cells. When Channel A opens, it allows an influx of calcium ions (Ca²⁺) into the cytosol. This rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺ triggers further calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) via ryanodine and inositol trisphosphate receptors, and can activate Channel B to sustain the calcium signal. Mitochondria help modulate this calcium signaling by buffering excess Ca²⁺, which influences both energy production and cellular responses.

In mitochondria, calcium activates Krebs cycle enzymes (isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase), enhancing ATP production. Also, in these cells, calcium release triggers insulin release in response to high glucose levels.

Mitochondrial calcium in pancreatic beta cells was measured using a fluorescence microscope with a calcium sensor. Inhibitors used: Inhibitor X (Channel B blocker) and Inhibitor Y (Channel A blocker). Results are shown in the graph below:

Figure 1. Calcium concentration under different conditions. A - control, B - inhibitor X, C - inhibitor Y, D - 30mM K+, E - calcium concentration (a.u.), F - time (mins). (cell media before D is applied: 2mM Ca2+, 5mM K+, low glucose)

A. In figure 1, cells depolarize after addition of 30mM K+.
B. From the experiment data provided we can conclude that the Channel A is ligand-gated.
C. If we performed a new experiment and replaced 30 mM K with high glucose in control conditions, the calcium concentration would not increase after high glucose stimulation.
D. If the same experiment as in Figure 1 was conducted in 0mM Ca2+ media, the response of the control cells would show a similar response to the inhibitor Y graph in Figure 1.

item.title: Q5 — Ketogenic Diet Metabolism and Catecholamine Seizure Latency
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Bioenergetics & Central Metabolism Overview

Ketogenic (high-fat, low-carbohydrate) diet is an efficient treatment for recurrent seizures, as in epilepsy. Ketogenic diet is thought to exert its effect via a metabolic pathway shown in Figure 1, as it leads to a production of beta-hydroxybutyrate. Increasing the number of reactions in a biochemical pathway decreases its overall reaction rate.

Figure 1. Glycolysis and ketolysis both feed into the TCA cycle via acetyl-CoA (reaction 1) and citrate (reaction 2); TCA-cycle intermediates alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate connect to the glutamate/GABA/aspartate shunt (reaction 3).

Dopamine is known to play a role in muscle control (e.g., its deficiency is one of the causes of Parkinson’s disease). A study investigated the interaction of catecholamines (dopamine, noradrenaline, and adrenaline) with a ketogenic diet. The study used Dbh knockout (Dbh-/-) and heterozygote (Dbh+/-) mice that were fed with either a ketogenic or normal diet. To estimate the efficacy of the diet in each group, they were introduced to fluorothyl (a seizure-inducing agent), and the latency to the first seizure was measured.

Figure 2. A Metabolism of catecholamines. B Seizure latency threshold (in milliseconds) after provocation with fluorothyl in Dbh +/- and -/- mice fed either the standard or ketogenic diet. Asterisk indicates a significant difference.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. A ketogenic diet facilitates the conversion of alpha-ketoglutarate to glutamate.
B. A mutation reducing the Km of the enzyme that catalyzes reaction 2 in Figure 1 decreases the value of the seizure latency (in milliseconds) in (Dbh+/-) mice with a ketogenic diet.
C. L-DOPA can be used as both an anti-convulsant and a treatment for Parkinson's disease.

item.title: Q6 — ProQC — Synthetic Toehold-Switch Quality Control of Translation
item.description:
Theoretical B Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Recombinant DNA & Biotechnology Techniques

ProQC is a synthetic biology tool used for the quality control of protein expression. ProQC consists of a synthetic gene-expression complex that only allows the expression of gene of interest (GOI)-encoded protein only from the full-length mRNAs. It is composed of two parts: a toehold switch containing a ribosome binding site (RBS) at the 5’ end of the GOI, and a cis-trigger at the 3’ end of the GOI, both under the same promoter. The sequence of the cis-trigger is reverse complementary to the toehold switch. When the toehold switch portion of the synthetic cassette is free, it forms a hairpin-like structure that blocks the RBS sequence.

Figure 1. Schematic diagram of one of the possible conformations of the ProQC system.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. The ProQC system allows translation only when the cis-trigger binds to the toehold switch.
B. The ProQC system increases the yield of functional proteins and reduces the waste of cellular resources.
C. This system is not necessary in eukaryotic cells.
D. In the ProQC system, the RBS in the toehold switch can be unblocked by trigger RNA transcribed separately from the ProQC system.

item.description:

DNA Structure & Replication

DNA fiber assay is used to study various aspects of DNA synthesis, such as replication speed, replication origin firing, and replication termination. It utilizes modified nucleotides to visualize the progression of DNA replication directly. In this assay, cellular DNA is sequentially labeled with chloro-deoxyuridine (CldU) followed by iodo-deoxyuridine (IdU), each for an equal period. Upon replication, cells incorporate these modified nucleotides into newly synthesized DNA. Next, cells are lysed and individual DNA fibers are stretched on a microscopic slide, followed by CldU (red) and IdU (blue) antibody staining. Finally, DNA fibers are visualized by fluorescent microscopy.

Figure 1. Panels A-F represent replicated DNA segments. Each panel shows a single uninterrupted DNA molecule labeled with CldU (red) followed by IdU (blue). The white bar at the bottom right of each panel is a scale bar of 10 μm. The DNA in all panels is from the same organism.

A. Panel A can represent replication progression from a single replication fork, while panel B shows replication progression from two forks.
B. Both panels C and E demonstrate replication termination.
C. In panel B, CldU is incorporated into either a leading or lagging strand of DNA but not into both.
D. The DNA belongs to a bacterial species.
